elements.element: Customer may assign to an affiliate without consent.
elements.evidence: Second paragraph of 18.9 requires consent for affiliate assignments: "either Party shall have the right to assign this Agreement to an Affiliate, with the prior written consent of the other Party (which shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed)", and the tax proviso lets the other Party refuse outright. No consent-free affiliate route was added.

elements.element: Customer may assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.
elements.evidence: 18.9: "either Party may assign this Agreement without the other Party's consent to an entity that acquires substantially all of the business or assets of the assigning Party, whether by merger, acquisition or otherwise".

elements.element: Vendor may not assign without Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: The same mutual carve-out lets Array (Vendor) assign to an acquirer of substantially all its business or assets without Ono's consent, so the Vendor-side consent gate is not absolute.

elements.element: Customer's consent to Vendor assignment is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: Inserted into the first sentence of 18.9: "without the written consent of the other Party hereto, which shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed"; the affiliate sentence carries the same standard.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: No competitor bar appears anywhere in 18.9/18.10; 18.10 only imposes firewall procedures on a Change in Control of Array, it does not prohibit assignment to an Ono competitor.

elements.element: Customer's change of control gives Vendor no termination right.
elements.evidence: 18.10 addresses only a Change in Control of Array and imposes firewalls; the cited operative text contains no Vendor termination or re-pricing right triggered by a change of control of Ono (Customer).

elements.element: Both parties may assign to a successor.
elements.evidence: 18.9 first sentence exception is expressly mutual: "either Party may assign this Agreement without the other Party's consent to an entity that acquires substantially all of the business or assets of the assigning Party, whether by merger, acquisition or otherwise".

elements.element: A successor assignment requires written notice.
elements.evidence: The carve-out is conditioned on "the acquiring party agrees in a writing delivered to the non-assigning Party to assume all of the rights and obligations of the assigning Party" — a writing that must reach the non-assigning Party, which supplies written notice in substance (indeed more than notice).

"This Agreement may not be assigned by either Party to any Third Party without the written consent of the other Party hereto..." and the affiliate route also requires "the prior written consent of the other Party" — no retained no-consent non-successor exception exists.

elements.element: Consent to other assignments is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: Redline adds "which shall not be unreasonably withheld or delayed" to the general Third Party consent gate; the affiliate consent sentence already carries the identical standard, and the retained tax proviso is itself reasonableness-qualified ("reasonably believes such assignment could result in material adverse tax consequences"), so it does not contradict the new standard.

reasons: Fallback level is complete: mutual successor carve-out, a writing delivered to the non-assigning Party on successor assignment, a consent gate for all other (including affiliate) assignments, and now an express reasonableness standard on that gate.

Preferred level fails on three elements the drafter must repair if pressed: (i) affiliate assignments still require the other Party's prior written consent rather than being consent-free for Customer, (ii) Vendor retains a consent-free successor assignment right so "Vendor may not assign without Customer's consent" is untrue, and (iii) no prohibition on Vendor assigning to an Ono competitor exists (18.10 only imposes firewalls on an Array Change in Control).

Minimality holds: the only operative change is the eight-word reasonableness qualifier in the first sentence of 18.9. The successor carve-out, the affiliate mechanic (including the guarantee and tax provisos), the competition-law sentence and the successors-and-assigns sentence are all retained verbatim. "or delayed" is a de minimis parallel to the identical formula already used in the affiliate sentence and does not create a new requirement outside the checklist.

Intent is preserved: no defined term is orphaned, no cross-reference dangles, and the retained affiliate tax proviso is reasonableness-based, so it does not contradict the newly inserted "not unreasonably withheld or delayed" standard applicable to Third Party assignments.

The classification as a deviation is defensible but marginal — the sole fallback gap was the unqualified consent standard; the change-of-control walk-away trigger is absent, so severity should be dialled down.
